summary: A free California Campfire Permit is required before you may have a campfire, camp stove, lantern or barbeque -- but holding one does NOT mean fires are allowed where you're going. Local restrictions override it. Two different permits exist; for everywhere this project covers, take the one for federal- and state-controlled lands, not the private-lands one.
detail: TWO PERMIT TYPES, and the wrong one is not a valid document. CAL FIRE issues one permit for federal- and state-controlled lands, covering campfires, barbeques and portable stoves, and a separate one for private lands, which additionally requires written permission from the landowner. Both carry the same caveat that local burn restrictions may apply. Every trailhead in this project sits on federal land -- national forest, national park, BLM, or the Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit -- except two on East Bay Regional Park District land (Del Valle and Stanford Ave), which is a special district fitting neither category cleanly; which permit applies there is not confirmed. The same portal also issues permits for burning debris, which is a different product and not what a backcountry traveller needs. THE PERMIT IS A PRECONDITION, NOT AN AUTHORISATION: CAL FIRE's own guidance says to check local rules, since many areas restrict or ban campfires outright, especially at elevation or in high fire danger. Where a wilderness bans fires, the permit still matters for a camp stove. YOU MUST CARRY IT: Eldorado NF states the permit has to be available for rangers and other officials to check while you are camping, so an unproduced permit is a permit you do not have. The lantern question is settled: CAL FIRE's permits FAQ omits lanterns from its enumeration, but the campfire-safety page and Eldorado NF's own FAQ both include them, so the fuller list stands on two sources against one summary. The issuing forest states it is also required in some developed campgrounds -- being in a campground is not a reliable exemption. Free, valid for a full calendar year (January 1 to December 31), and available from CAL FIRE, US Forest Service or BLM offices as well as online. The signer must be 18 or older, so a group of minors cannot self-issue. Obtain it at readyforwildfire.org/permits, which links to the portal at permit.preventwildfiresca.org. NOTE: Eldorado NF's own camping page cites 'www.preventwildfiresca.org', which does not resolve -- readyforwildfire.org is the working entry point.

summary: Dispersed camping outside a developed campground is limited to 10 days per ranger district per calendar year.
detail: Most Eldorado NF land is open to free dispersed camping unless specifically prohibited. There is no trash service -- pack it in, pack it out -- and no potable water, so bring your own rather than relying on lakes, streams or springs. Remove all equipment and garbage when leaving. Eldorado NF's FAQ confirms dispersed camping is allowed forest-wide and restates that your group is responsible for all trash and should take it home. It also says to check with a Ranger District office for fire restrictions before you go, and that a campfire permit is required for a cooking appliance, lantern or campfire even when dispersed.

summary: Campfires are prohibited year-round throughout Desolation Wilderness. Camp stoves are permitted.
detail: A stove still requires the separate California Campfire Permit that applies statewide.

Confirm rental terms before relying on them.

summary: Maximum group size is 12 people together at any time, children included in the count.
detail: recreation.gov's booking widget enforces this as a hard cap of 12 group members per permit, and the cap is flat rather than per zone -- it reads '12 max' whichever destination zone is selected. Note what the figure is sourced to. A destination zone is the OVERNIGHT quota mechanism: you book a zone for your first night. So this confirms the overnight cap. NO SOURCE ON HAND STATES A GROUP SIZE FOR DESOLATION DAY USE, which is a separate, free, self-issued permit that is not booked through this widget. Do not assume it is also 12: neighbouring Mokelumne, administered by the same forest, caps day hikes at 12 and overnight groups at 8, so the two numbers demonstrably differ within one agency.

summary: You may gather downed firewood while camping without a permit, but may not cut any tree, and may not take gathered wood home.
detail: Bringing firewood from outside the forest is prohibited, because it transports non-native pests. Buy it from the camp host or from a grocery store, where it is vetted pest-free. This permits the gathering, not the fire: Desolation and Mokelumne both ban campfires outright, and the statewide campfire permit is still required for a stove or lantern.

summary: Dogs must be physically restrained on a leash under six feet for the whole visit -- not merely under voice control.
detail: Eldorado NF states this as a forest-wide requirement, and it is stricter than the "under control at all times" wording on the Desolation permit page. Bag dog waste and put it in a trash receptacle or take it home; in wilderness, bury it in a cat hole off trail and away from water. Off-leash dogs threaten wildlife and endanger or inconvenience other visitors.

summary: A firearm may be carried only if it is visible and unloaded, unless you are actively hunting. California state firearm law applies.
detail: This governs carrying; discharge is restricted separately (Desolation bars any discharge within 150 yards of a campsite or occupied area). Concealed or loaded carry outside active hunting is not permitted here.

summary: Drones are allowed on the forest but NOT over congressionally designated wilderness, which includes Desolation and Mokelumne.
detail: Since almost every objective in this project lies inside designated wilderness, the practical answer for a summit flight is no. Drones are also barred wherever a Temporary Flight Restriction is in place, which is routine over active wildfires -- check before flying in fire season.

summary: Campfires are prohibited everywhere in Mokelumne Wilderness, year-round. Camp stoves and lanterns are allowed.
detail: The stated reason is ecological, not just fire risk: dead and downed wood is critical habitat for alpine species, and its decomposition drives the nutrient value of the soils high-altitude vegetation depends on. So Eldorado NF's forest-wide allowance on gathering downed firewood does not translate into a fire here. A stove or lantern still needs the statewide California Campfire Permit, and the permit instructions add a specific requirement: it must be carried to use an on/off switch style gas camp stove.

summary: Maximum group size is 8 people overnight and 12 for a day hike.
detail: The day-use figure is higher than the overnight one, which is easy to get backwards. Groups may not camp or travel within one mile of a related group -- splitting a large party does not evade the limit. If your group is too large, the forest asks you to reduce it, split to different areas, or choose somewhere outside the wilderness. Where multiple groups do hike the same trail, stagger start times by thirty minutes.

summary: Camp at least 100 ft from any stream, lake or designated trail; the permit page asks for 200 ft from water.
detail: The two official sources differ on the water setback: the 2025 regulations sheet says 100 ft, the permit page (last updated 2026-03-03) says at least 200 ft. Use 200 ft and you satisfy both. Three named places are stricter still: no camping within 300 ft of Emigrant Lake or within a quarter mile of Frog Lake, both to let shorelines recover, and no overnight backpacking around Woods Lake at all, where camping is confined to the developed campground. The Emigrant and Frog Lake limits lift only when there is snow on the ground, and then only on a durable surface -- do not dig down to bare earth. Stay on existing tent pads.

summary: Bear canisters are RECOMMENDED, not required -- counterbalance hanging is an accepted alternative.
detail: This is a real difference from neighbouring Desolation, where a hard-sided canister is mandatory and non-compliance carries fines up to $5,000. Do not carry a Desolation habit into Mokelumne as an assumption in either direction. Canisters are available for free loan at the Amador Ranger District office. Bears are active at higher elevations than in the past because of poorly stored food, and are drawn to toothpaste and deodorant as much as to food. Empty your pack of anything scented, and leave pack and tent zippers open so curious animals can investigate without tearing the fabric.

summary: Mechanized and motorized equipment is prohibited, including bicycles, strollers and game carts.
detail: The full list given is bicycles, vehicles, hang gliders, over-snow vehicles including snowmobiles, strollers, chainsaws and game carts. Strollers and game carts surprise people: the rule is about mechanical transport, not about engines, so a wheeled device with no motor is still barred.

summary: Bury human and dog waste 6-8 inches deep, at least 200 ft from water, campsites and trails. Pack out toilet paper.
detail: When there is snow on the ground, pack out both the toilet paper and the waste -- burying in snow does not work. Leaving refuse, debris or litter is prohibited outright; pack out everything you pack in. Digging animals will expose anything buried shallow.

summary: Treat all water by boiling or filtering. No soap of any kind in any water source, biodegradable included.
detail: Giardia lamblia and Cryptosporidium are present even in remote lakes and streams. Beyond soap, the regulations name insect repellent and sunscreen as contaminants -- rinse them off away from the water before swimming, and wash cookware well away from any source.

summary: Damaging or removing any natural OR HISTORIC feature is prohibited.
detail: The historic clause is broader than the equivalent Desolation rule, which covers natural features only. Mining-era and emigrant-trail relics are protected here. Leave wildflowers, and avoid trampling lakeshore vegetation.

summary: Do not hitch, tether or hobble stock within 200 ft of water or 100 ft of a campsite, and never tie directly to trees.
detail: Tying directly to a tree is allowed only briefly while loading, unloading, or resting on the move. Carry weed-free supplemental or processed feed such as alfalfa pellets or crimped oats. In the Mokelumne Canyon and below Telephone Gulch in Lower Summit City Canyon, overnight camping with stock is restricted to named corridors: in the Munson Meadow / Camp Irene / Lake Valley corridor only Camp Irene, one stock group at a time; in Summit City Canyon from Telephone Gulch to where the maintained trail crosses Summit City Creek; and from Hermit Valley trailhead to roughly half a mile below Deer Creek. Two nights maximum, four animals per group. In the Round Top Special Interest Area stock must stay on trails and no grazing is permitted, to protect the botanical values it was designated for.

summary: Dogs must be physically restrained on a leash no longer than six feet for the whole visit.
detail: Three Eldorado NF documents state this at three different scopes, broadening over time: the 2025 regulations sheet applies it to the Carson Pass Management Area, the 2025 permit instructions to the Mokelumne Wilderness and the CPMA, and the forest's 2026 FAQ to the forest generally. The CPMA requirement is certain in all three. Owners are responsible for their pets and for packing out or burying dog waste. The forest suggests asking at the Carson Pass Information Station or Amador District office for areas better suited to dogs than the CPMA.

summary: Hunting and fishing are both allowed, in the wilderness included, under California state law.
detail: Seasons, limits and licensing are set by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, not by the forest, and licences come from CDFW online or through a licence agent. Salt Springs State Game Refuge is closed to hunting. A wilderness permit is not a hunting or fishing licence.

summary: Maximum group size is 15 people and 25 stock -- except the Sawtooth Ridge Zone, which caps at 8 people and allows no stock.
detail: The Sawtooth Ridge Zone covers the Matterhorn, Whorl and Virginia Peak area reached from the Robinson Creek / Twin Lakes trailhead. The stricter cap follows you there even on a permit issued for the wider wilderness, and it still applies when a Hoover permit is honoured for continuous travel into a neighbouring unit.

summary: Maximum 25 head of stock.
Campfires are banned above 9,000 ft and within half a mile of Emigrant Lake, whatever permit you hold.
detail: Separate from the outright year-round ban in Mokelumne Wilderness next door. The statewide California Campfire Permit is still required for a stove wherever fires themselves are barred.

summary: Maximum group size is 15 people, day or overnight, with 25 stock; groups must stay a mile apart.
detail: Applies in Emigrant and Carson-Iceberg Wildernesses.

summary: Camping is prohibited within 100 ft of lakes, streams and trails.
Bear canisters are NOT required in these Stanislaus wildernesses.
detail: Stated as a non-requirement rather than left silent, because silence reads as unknown and the answer differs sharply nearby: Yosemite requires canisters, and Desolation requires a hard-sided one on pain of a $5,000 fine. Carrying one anyway is still sensible where bears are active.

summary: Campfires may be prohibited for dispersed camping depending on current fire danger.
detail: Conditional rather than fixed, so check the current restriction before planning on a fire; a stove needs the statewide California Campfire Permit either way.

summary: Maximum 14 consecutive days in the forest.
At campgrounds, dogs, cats or other animals must be attended and either leashed, or contained within a vehicle, tent or other type of physical confinement.
detail: Confinement is an accepted alternative to a leash here, not a concession -- a leash-only reading of this rule would be wrong. The ordinance names cats directly ('dogs, cats, or other animals'), so this is not a dog rule being read across to another species. Two limits sit beside it that are NOT species-neutral, and the difference is the ordinance's, not this project's: the three-per-person cap in 801.2(d) is written for dogs, and the leash-optional allowance for undeveloped areas in 801.3 opens 'A dog may run at large', so a cat has no off-leash provision anywhere in the District. Whether the campground itself accepts a given animal is a separate question from this rule and is not answered here: the Ohlone Wilderness Trail backpack camps are reported to bar dogs outright, which this project has not confirmed against a source.

summary: In developed areas -- which include every campground, picnic area, parking lot, public road and paved multi-use trail -- and within approximately 200 feet of any parking lot, trail head or staging area, a dog, cat or other animal must be securely leashed and under control.
detail: The leash may be no longer than six feet. An extendable leash is permitted only if it is not extended beyond six feet in a leash-required area. An electronic collar is explicitly excluded from counting as a restraint: the ordinance defines leashed as tied or otherwise physically restrained, '(excluding electronic collars)'. The 200 ft radius is measured from the parking lot, trail head or staging area, or as posted, so it applies before you have started walking. Attachment C lists all campgrounds among the areas where this is required. Attachment C also states that on trails crossing or entering lands owned by others, dog owners comply with THAT agency's rules, naming East Bay Municipal Utility District land, San Francisco Public Utility land and Mount Diablo State Park. This is not a formality at Anthony Chabot: the Chabot-to-Garin Regional Trail crosses onto EBMUD watershed land, where a separate trail use permit is required (permit_group ebmud_trail) and EBMUD's rules govern, not these.

summary: No dog, cat or other animal is permitted -- even securely leashed -- in any swimming pool, bathing beach, designated nature study area, wetland or marsh area, or golf course.
detail: Del Valle Beaches/Swim Area is named in Attachment B, which matters directly: Del Valle is this project's East Bay trailhead and its only drive-in campground. Round Valley Regional Preserve is prohibited outright as a wildlife protection area for listed species at risk, as is the Tilden Botanical Garden and Nature Area. Service animals trained to assist disabled persons, and whose presence is reasonably necessary, are exempt. A tension worth knowing rather than resolving here: section 801.1 bars 'dog, cat, or other animal', while the attachment enumerating the places is headed 'Specific Parks or Areas of Parks Where Dogs Are Prohibited'. The operative sentence is the broader one. EBRPD's booking system draws a line the ordinance does not spell out: EMOTIONAL SUPPORT ANIMALS ARE NOT SERVICE ANIMALS for this exemption. It states that dogs, including emotional support animals, are barred from the swim beach, swim area, select trails and cabins, while service animals with specialized training are permitted in all locations. Someone travelling with an ESA is covered by the general pet rules, not by the exemption.
citation: EBRPD Ordinance 38 s.801.1 and Attachment B

summary: No dog, cat or other animal may be left unattended at any parkland unless it is contained.
detail: District-wide, not a campground rule -- it applies to a car in a trailhead parking lot as much as to a campsite. Abandoning an animal is separately prohibited, and the ordinance names cats in that rule too: an abandoned animal is live-trapped and relocated or turned over to Animal Control. Feeding feral or wild animals, which the ordinance states includes cats, is prohibited at all times.

summary: Any person bringing a dog onto park property must immediately remove its excrement and place it in a garbage can or carry it out.
detail: Written for dogs specifically. The ordinance states no equivalent duty for other animals, which is an absence in the source rather than permission -- pack it out on the same terms.

summary: Maximum 8 occupants per family campground site.
detail: A per-site cap, distinct from a per-permit or per-party limit. Groups larger than this are directed to group campsites, which have their own minimums and maximums.

summary: Camping is allowed only in designated areas and only with a valid District permit. Stay is limited to 15 consecutive days per park, or 30 total days per year, with a two-day minimum break after the first 15-day visit.
detail: 'Camp', 'camping', 'campsite' and 'campground' are defined to cover all types of camping -- traditional tent, RV, cabin and walk-in sites alike -- so neither the stay limit nor the occupancy cap can be read as applying to only one style. All persons at a campsite may be removed for a violation of state law, this ordinance or campground rules, and for 15 days afterwards the person removed may not reserve or occupy any campsite in the District, with no refund of unused camping, vehicle or other fees. HOW THE LIMIT IS COUNTED, which Ordinance 38 does not say and the booking system does: the 15 consecutive and 30 total nights are counted PER HOUSEHOLD ADDRESS, customer name, primary occupant or registered vehicle -- not per person. A family cannot reset the clock by booking in a different member's name, and the same vehicle turning up is the same household. WALK-IN AND DROP-IN STAYS COUNT TOWARD IT too, so nights taken without a reservation are not free of the tally. The 2-day break is stated by the booking system as 48 hours, which is the same thing said in hours.

summary: Open outdoor fires are allowed only in the facilities provided and designated for them, and no fire may be left unattended. Personal gas or propane camp stoves, portable barbecues and hibachis are permitted, but not on beaches or anywhere posted 'No BBQ'.
detail: This is the local restriction that sits on top of the statewide California Campfire Permit: holding the permit does not make a fire lawful here. A personal appliance must be placed where it will not scorch lawns or table tops and at least 30 feet from flammable material such as grass, weeds, wood chips, brush or buildings, and burning fuel must be thoroughly extinguished before disposal in an existing fireplace, fire pit or grill -- never in a garbage can. Smoking is prohibited district-wide, vapor devices included; that is a standing ban, not a fire-season one. During declared fire season, extreme conditions may eliminate all open flames for any purpose, or close the park.

summary: Ordinance 38 allows a generator unless it disturbs other campers. THE BOOKING SYSTEM SAYS 'NO GAS GENERATORS', flatly. The two do not agree -- see the ebrpd-generators thread.
detail: Stated as a disturbance test rather than posted quiet hours, so it applies at any time of day. Covers radio, television, tape or record players and speaker systems as well as generators. THE CONTRADICTION, ADDED 2026-09-16: Ordinance 38 s.400.2 and s.908.2 state a DISTURBANCE TEST -- no generator or sound-amplification device may be operated in a campground if it disturbs other campers, which permits a quiet one at any hour. EBRPD's own booking system, in the campground rules attached to every reservation, states 'No gas generators' with no condition at all. A camper relying on the ordinance brings one; a camper relying on the rules they agreed to at booking does not. Both are EBRPD. The safer reading is the flat ban, because the booking rules are the terms the reservation is made under, but that is a judgement and not what the ordinance says. Note also that the booking rules speak of GAS generators specifically, where the ordinance is silent on fuel -- so a battery power station may be outside both, and nothing read says so.

summary: A juvenile -- any unmarried person under 18 -- may not camp on District parkland unless accompanied by a parent or guardian, or, as part of a permitted group, supervised by at least one responsible adult over 21 for every ten juveniles.
detail: Agency-wide under Ordinance 38 s.400.4, not a rule of any one campground, which is why it sits here rather than in a campground's notes: it governs the family campground and the backpack camps as much as the group camps. EBRPD's booking system restates it in the terms a reservation holder meets -- juveniles under 18 accompanied by a parent, legal guardian or other responsible adult aged 21 or over, and large groups needing one adult per ten juveniles. The 21-and-over bar matters: an 18-year-old is an adult for the purposes of being unaccompanied, but not for the purposes of supervising anyone else.

summary: NO campfires and NO barbecues at Black Diamond Mines, at any time and in any season. Camp stoves are acceptable.
detail: STRICTER THAN THE DISTRICT RULE IT SITS ON TOP OF, and that is why it is scoped to the park. EBRPD's own agency-wide rule permits portable barbecues and hibachis subject to clearance, so a reader shown only that rule arrives here with a barbecue they may not use. Neither of this park's two camping areas has any fire ring. Note the difference from a fire ban declared for conditions: this is not seasonal and does not lift.

summary: No alcohol at all is allowed at Black Diamond Mines.
detail: Also stricter than the District, and the contrast is sharp enough to catch someone out: Anthony Chabot allows beer and wine at campsites and picnic areas for over-21s, and Ordinance 38 bars alcohol only in non-designated areas. Here there is no designated area. Star Mine takes organized educational groups only, which is the likely reason.

summary: Haul out all your own garbage and equipment -- there is no rubbish collection at either camping area.
detail: Leave no trace, stated by the booking system and echoed by the park's own page for Star Mine. Pairs with the water situation: Star Mine has no water at all, and Stewartville's is for horses and non-potable, so everything comes in and goes out with the party.

summary: Dogs must be leashed, six-foot maximum, at ALL times on four named stretches of trail: the whole Tavan Trail; Diablo View Trail between Alhambra Creek Trail and Hidden Pond Trail; Alhambra Creek Trail from the Alhambra Creek Staging Area south to the water trough; and Orchard Trail from Alhambra Creek Trail west to the Briones Road gate.
detail: SHARPENS ORDINANCE 38 ATTACHMENT C, which names 'designated sections of Alhambra Creek, Tavan, Diablo View and Orchard Trails in Briones Regional Park' without saying which sections. These are the sections. It matters because Briones is otherwise leash-optional undeveloped land under s.801.3, where a dog may run at large under control -- so these four stretches are the exception inside the exception, and they are marked by signage rather than being obvious from the map. SEPARATELY, cattle graze named trail areas here -- cows and calves in Tabletop, Spengler, Blue Oak, Buckeye, Sunrise and Lafayette Ridge, yearlings in Deer Creek, Pereirra, Valley and Briones Crest -- and s.801.21 requires any dog or other animal to be leashed and under complete control wherever grazing animals are present, which is a larger area than these four segments.

summary: No open fires or barbecues of ANY type at Sunol. Gas-fuelled stoves are permitted at Alameda Grove and School Camp ONLY.
detail: The second park-scoped fire ban in this project, and it is stricter than Black Diamond's: there, camp stoves are acceptable anywhere; here even a gas stove is confined to two named places, neither of which is Sunol Backpack Camp -- the camp this project actually holds, on the Ohlone Wilderness Trail. Read at agency scope alone, EBRPD's District-wide rule permits portable barbecues and hibachis subject to clearance, so a backpacker planning a hot meal at Sunol Backpack Camp on that basis plans something they may not do. POSTED AS A FIRE WARNING rather than in the park's camping text, so it reads as conditional; it is recorded as a standing rule because the wording names permanent exceptions by location rather than a date range, but whether it lifts outside fire season is NOT STATED and is worth asking.

summary: At a BACKPACK site the stay limit is 2 nights, except on the Ohlone Wilderness Trail -- Mission Peak, Sunol and Ohlone -- where up to 3 consecutive nights are allowed in order to walk the whole trail.
detail: A different limit from the family campground's 15 consecutive days, and it reaches seven camps this project already holds: Boyd, Stewart's, Maggie's Half Acre, Doe, Sunol Backpack, Eagle Springs and Round Valley. THE OHLONE EXCEPTION EXISTS FOR A REASON WORTH KNOWING: the trail is 28 miles, and two nights does not comfortably cover it, so the District allows a third specifically for a through-walk. Also one backpack site per household address, customer name, primary occupant or registered vehicle on any date; additional bookings are cancelled rather than queried. Stated by the booking system, which is where the District publishes backpack terms -- no ebparks.org page read here carries it.

summary: NO DOGS OVERNIGHT at the Mission Peak, Sunol and Ohlone Trail backpack sites. Other locations vary and must be checked per site.
detail: Scoped to the agency rather than a park because it names a CLASS OF SITE, not a place: the Ohlone corridor camps in this project are filed under Del Valle Regional Park, where the Del Valle Family Campground allows dogs, so a park-scoped rule would ban them at the wrong campground. Read it as naming its own sites. It is stricter than Ordinance 38 s.801.2(i), which permits a leashed or contained animal at campgrounds generally, and it is an overnight ban rather than a leash requirement -- a dog may walk the trail and may not sleep at the camp. The ordinance's own species wording does not carry here: the booking system says dogs, and whether a cat is covered is NOT STATED.

summary: At a BACKPACK site: no campfires and no charcoal barbecues. Camp stoves are permitted. No alcohol at all, beer and wine included.
detail: Backpack sites are treated as their own class District-wide, and both halves are stricter than the agency rule they sit under: Ordinance 38 s.404.1 permits portable barbecues subject to clearance, and the family campgrounds allow beer and wine for over-21s. The alcohol half is the one most likely to surprise, since Anthony Chabot's family sites permit it and its group sites permit it with an extra permit. Recorded under fire because that is the half with a category; the alcohol clause has no vocabulary of its own here.

summary: No dogs are allowed anywhere in Round Valley Regional Preserve, at any time.
detail: A whole-park ban, not a leash rule, and the reason is on the park's own page: the preserve holds the endangered San Joaquin kit fox at the northern extreme of its range, and DOGS CAN BE A DISEASE VECTOR to it. Ordinance 38 Attachment B already listed Round Valley as a wildlife protection area for listed species at risk; this states the ban plainly and gives it a cause. The backpack site's own listing permits HORSE only among pets. Nesting golden eagles, burrowing owls and the federally threatened California red-legged frog are also present.

summary: No hard alcohol anywhere. Beer and wine only, 21 and over, and only at campsites or picnic areas -- not in parking lots, on trails or at swim beaches. A GROUP CAMPSITE NEEDS AN ADDITIONAL BEER AND WINE PERMIT, bought in advance.
detail: The permit costs $25.00 and is bought by calling EBRPD Reservations; it cannot be added on arrival. So a group that brings beer without having phoned ahead is in breach even though beer is allowed. THIS DOES NOT REACH EVERY SITE IN THE DISTRICT. Two narrower rules override it and both are already recorded: Black Diamond Mines bans alcohol entirely at park scope, and EBRPD's backpack sites ban it entirely, beer and wine included. A camper who reads only this rule and goes to Stewartville is wrong. The District norm is beer and wine with a permit; the exceptions are where this project has looked hardest. A THIRD EXCEPTION, FOUND THE SAME DAY THIS RULE WAS FILED: Wee-Ta-Chi at Briones states 'ALCOHOL: Not permitted' on its own booking page. It is not recorded here because this table's narrowest scope is PARK and the ban is published for one site, while Briones' other two group camps publish no site notes at all -- so whether the ban is the site's or the park's cannot be told from what has been read. It sits on the Wee-Ta-Chi campground row instead. The count now stands at two recorded exceptions and one that has nowhere to go, which is what a missing scope level looks like from the inside.

summary: Fires only in designated areas, and only with wood you brought: commercially purchased wood, processed fire logs or cut lumber. COLLECTING WOOD IS PROHIBITED. Every fire must be attended by an adult and thoroughly extinguished on departure.
detail: This is the supply half of the fire question and it is separate from whether a fire is allowed at all -- Ordinance 38 s.404 governs where a fire may burn, this governs what may burn in it. A site with a fire circle and no wood for sale nearby is a site you carry fuel to. EBRPD also warns that fire restrictions may be in place during a stay, checked through its fire danger page, and its own cancellation terms give NO REFUND when restrictions tighten.

summary: No smoking and no vaping.
detail: Stated flatly in the booking system's campground rules, with no exception for a campsite and no designated area named.

summary: No limit on the NUMBER of tents at a site, but every tent must stand on dirt or a designated tent pad. NO TENTS ON LAWNS.
detail: Site sizes vary, so the binding constraint is ground rather than count: a party within its occupancy limit can still be unable to pitch what it brought. Relevant at the group camps here, which state tent pads only at Round Valley and Star Mine; the rest describe picnic tables and fire rings without saying what the ground is.

summary: Two vehicles per campsite. Group and backpack sites vary, and their own listings state the number.
detail: The per-site figure is the family default. The group sites read for this project each state their own and none matches it: Star Mine 7 parking spaces, Dairy Glen 10, Arroyo Flats 15 passes of which only 2 may park at the site. Where a group site states a figure, that figure governs and this one does not.

summary: A MAXIMUM OF TWO family campsites per household address, customer name, primary occupant or registered vehicle on any given date -- additional sites are CANCELLED. Other site types are limited to one per date per party, group, household or primary contact. A group larger than 16 should reserve a group campsite.
detail: The counting keys are the same four the stay limit uses, so a party cannot split a booking across names or vehicles to get a third site. It bites hardest against the release mechanics already recorded: reservations open by phone with a maximum of two per call, and this caps the household at two anyway. A party of twenty needing three family sites cannot legally have them under one household, which is what 'groups larger than 16 should reserve a group campsite' is really saying -- and 16 is not 17, the minimum most group sites here state, so a party of 17 is the smallest that fits both halves cleanly.

summary: MAXIMUM THREE DOGS PER SITE. Dogs must be confined to a vehicle or tent during quiet hours and must never be left unattended. Anyone with a noisy, vicious or uncontrollable dog will be asked to leave.
detail: A count limit, which none of the Ordinance 38 pets rules give -- those govern leashing, confinement and where an animal may go, not how many. NOTE WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY: this rule is written about DOGS, while Ordinance 38 s.801 is written about 'dog, cat or other animal'. Whether three is a cap on dogs or on animals is not stated, so a party bringing cats has no number here. Ask Reservations rather than reading the dog figure across. THE CONFINEMENT CLAUSE CHANGES WITH THE SITE, WHICH IS WORTH NOTICING: Garin's copy says a dog must be confined to a VEHICLE OR TENT during quiet hours; Reinhardt Redwood's says confined to a TENT. Reinhardt's three camps ban driving in, so there is no vehicle at the site to confine a dog in -- the rule text tracks the access mode. Reinhardt's version also adds that pets must be under voice control at all times and spells out where leashes are required: parking lots, within 200 feet of any trail or park entrance or as posted, picnic areas, developed areas such as lawns and play fields, on some trails, and wherever grazing animals are present.

summary: In the Redwood Creek Resource Protection Area, DOGS MUST BE ON LEASH on Stream Trail and Bridle Trail, and PEOPLE AND DOGS MUST STAY OUT OF THE CREEK and off the creek banks.
detail: Printed on the park's own map inside the marked protection area. It is stricter than the District's developed-areas leash rule, which lets a dog off leash on an undeveloped trail: here two named trails require a leash for their length. The creek ban covers people as well as dogs, which no other rule in this project does -- it is a habitat closure written as a use rule, and the park is the last stretch of spawning habitat the Fishway Interpretive Site on the same map exists to explain. Filed under pets because that is where the leash half belongs and this vocabulary has no habitat category; the human half is in the summary so it cannot be lost.

summary: FISHING IS NOT ALLOWED. The park page says not anywhere in the park; the booking system says not in Redwood Creek, 'either in the park OR ALONG REDWOOD ROAD'. The second is narrower about where and wider about how far.
detail: Stated flatly on the park page, with no season, no permit and no exception. It is the first fishing rule in this dataset and the first EBRPD rule of any kind that is a plain park-wide ban on an activity the District advertises elsewhere -- Garin and Dry Creek Pioneer both carry a Fishing activity icon. Consistent with the creek protection area on the map, though neither source says one causes the other. REFINED AND COMPLICATED THE SAME DAY. The park page's flat 'Fishing is not allowed in the park' and the campground rules' 'Fishing in Redwood Creek, either in the park or along Redwood Road' do not describe the same area. One bans fishing everywhere inside the boundary; the other bans it in one creek and follows that creek OUTSIDE the park along a public road, which no other rule in this dataset does -- a park's rule reaching past its own boundary. No conflict thread is opened because the two overlap rather than contradict: inside the park the creek is covered either way, and nothing anywhere says fishing IS permitted. Both are stored so that a reader by the roadside culvert knows the ban follows them there.

summary: A prohibited list the campground rules carry and Ordinance 38's summaries here do not: NO DRONES. No hanging anything in or from trees or structures. No wading or swimming in undesignated areas. No feeding or approaching wildlife. No releasing animals into parklands. No damaging plants or geological or archaeological features. NO BALLOONS OR PINATAS.
detail: Read on Reinhardt Redwood's listing, in the block EBRPD attaches to reservations rather than in the ordinance. Two of these matter more than they look. 'RELEASING ANIMALS INTO PARKLANDS' is the only rule in this dataset about bringing an animal you do not intend to take home, and it sits beside the pets rules without being one. 'No balloons or pinatas' reads as trivia and is a litter rule: both shed fragments that are eaten by wildlife, which is the same concern as the feeding ban two clauses earlier. Stored at agency scope because the block is District boilerplate, with the usual caveat that it was read on one park's page. Leave no trace and pack out what you pack in is stated in the same block; bulky items must go out with you rather than into the bins.

summary: SEVEN NIGHTS A MONTH AND THIRTY A YEAR at this park's group sites, which is not the District's 15-consecutive-days figure and is much tighter.
detail: 'Site reservations: Reservations are limited to one (1)/date per party/group, household address, primary contact, etc. 7 night maximum/month; 30 nights/year.' THIS IS NOT A CONTRADICTION OF ebrpd-camping-stay-limit, on the best reading: Garin's copy of the same block says 'Cabin, group, backpack, or equestrian site stay limitations VARY BY SITE TYPE', and Ordinance 38's 15 consecutive days is the general cap. Seven nights a month looks like the group-site figure that sentence is pointing at. THE READING IS A JUDGEMENT AND THE SCOPE SHOWS IT: this is filed at PARK scope because only this park's page states a number, and regulations.csv has no scope for a class of site. If another park's group listing states seven nights, it belongs at agency scope. The 30 nights a year matches the ordinance exactly, which is the reason to think the monthly figure is real rather than a transcription slip.
